panels.description: redis_memory_used_bytes / redis_memory_max_bytes, expressed as percent. `--maxmemory` is Redis's own ceiling; once this line crosses 100% Redis returns OOM-on-write errors (with `--maxmemory-policy noeviction` no keys are dropped, the writer sees the error). Threshold-shaded: green <70%, yellow 70-85%, orange 85-95%, red >95%. Sustained red means raise the pod limit + `--maxmemory`, or trim the working set.
panels.title: Memory % of maxmemory cap

panels.description: redis_evicted_keys_total: counter of keys removed by Redis's eviction policy. With `--maxmemory-policy noeviction` (our setting) this MUST stay at 0; a non-zero value means either the policy was changed or a different Redis instance is being scraped. Background turns red the moment it crosses 0.
panels.title: Evicted keys (cumulative)

panels.description: Current redis_memory_used_bytes: bytes Redis tracks as in-use (working set). Pairs with the % chart on the left; this is the absolute value. Source: redis_memory_used_bytes.
panels.title: Memory used now

panels.description: Three views of Redis memory. `used` (blue) = bytes Redis tracks as in-use (its working set). `RSS` (orange) = kernel-resident, includes allocator overhead. `peak` (purple) = high-water mark since process start. used and RSS diverging is the fragmentation signal; peak climbing without flat periods is the address-space-growth signature. Sources: redis_memory_used_bytes, redis_memory_used_rss_bytes, redis_memory_used_peak_bytes.
panels.title: Memory composition: used / RSS / peak

panels.description: rate(redis_cpu_user_seconds_total + redis_cpu_sys_seconds_total)[1m]: Redis process CPU in cores. Redis is single-threaded for command execution, so this is bounded at ~1.0 core in steady state. Threshold lines mark danger zones. Sustained >0.5 means commands or Lua scripts are CPU-bound; >0.8 means we're about to saturate the single thread and tail latency will climb. Sources: redis_cpu_user_seconds_total, redis_cpu_sys_seconds_total.
panels.title: Redis CPU usage (user + sys)

panels.description: rate(redis_commands_processed_total[5m]): total Redis commands processed per second across all clients. Tracks the crawler's actual Redis load (~50-200 ops/sec/worker is typical: claim + ack + advance_wake + 50 submits per fetched page). A drop to zero while the crawler is fetching = clients lost connection. Source: redis_commands_processed_total.
panels.title: Commands per second

panels.description: hits / (hits + misses) over the last 5 minutes. Reflects only commands that look up a key (GET, HGET, EXISTS); BF.ADD / RPUSH / ZADD aren't counted. For us this is mostly the `urls` HGET path at claim time. Threshold-shaded: red <50%, yellow 50-90%, green >=90%. A low ratio means we're frequently looking up keys that don't exist (could indicate orphan IDs in queues; investigate via the urls hash size). Source: redis_keyspace_hits_total / (hits + misses).
panels.title: Keyspace hit rate

panels.description: Clients connected to Redis (blue) and a subset of those currently blocked on a command like BLPOP / BRPOP (yellow). Connected should roughly track the sum of all pool sizes across the crawler + outbox publisher. Blocked > 0 is rare for us (we don't use blocking commands); a sustained value means a stuck consumer. Sources: redis_connected_clients, redis_blocked_clients.
panels.title: Connected clients + blocked

panels.description: rate(redis_rejected_connections_total[5m]): connections refused because Redis was at `maxclients`. Should be 0 in steady state; sustained non-zero = `maxclients` is too low for the crawler's pool sizing. Default `maxclients` is 10000 which is well above our needs, so this firing usually points to a connection leak in the crawler. Source: redis_rejected_connections_total.
panels.title: Rejected connections (rate)

panels.description: redis_rdb_changes_since_last_save: writes accumulated since the last successful RDB snapshot. Drops to 0 every time a snapshot fires (per the `save N M` thresholds in REDIS_ARGS: `save 60 10000`, `save 300 10`, `save 900 1`). The sawtooth pattern is healthy. A monotonically climbing line that never resets means bgsave is failing - cross-check with the next panel. Source: redis_rdb_changes_since_last_save.
panels.title: RDB changes since last save

panels.description: Seconds since the most recent successful RDB snapshot. Indirectly tells you how much data we'd lose on a Redis crash (everything since the last snapshot). For our `save 60 10000 / save 300 10 / save 900 1` cadence this typically stays under 15 min. Threshold-shaded: green <5min, yellow 5-15min, red >30min. Source: time() - redis_rdb_last_save_timestamp_seconds.
panels.title: Time since last RDB save

panels.description: redis_db_keys{db}: total number of top-level keys in each Redis database. For us this is `db0` (the only DB we use). Includes our per-shard host_queues, wake/ready/inflight, urls hashes, and bloom filters. Growing without flat periods is the signal that submission rate is outpacing claim rate. Source: redis_db_keys.
panels.title: Total keys per DB

panels.description: Number of keys in each namespace. host_queue and host_count are per-host (climb with unique hosts seen); urls / wake / inflight / ready / seen are per-shard (cap at 8 each). A surprising climb in the per-shard groups = something didn't get deleted.
panels.title: Key count by key group

panels.description: Bytes consumed by each crawlrs key namespace (host_queue / wake / ready / inflight / urls / host_count / seen). Stacked area so total = total tracked. A group climbing without a matching counterpart shrinking = where memory growth is going. Requires `--check-key-groups` on the redis_exporter sidecar.
panels.title: Memory by key group

panels.description: Instant snapshot, sorted by current memory. Quick answer to 'which namespace is biggest right now'.
panels.title: Top key groups by memory (now)

panels.description: Bytes per shard's URL HASH (content-addressed payload store). Each shard's HASH should drop after URLs are acked; a monotonic climb is an unack'd URL leak. 8 series (one per shard); the {key} label is the full Redis key including the {<tag>} hash-slot.
panels.title: URLs HASH: memory per shard

panels.description: Number of leases held per shard. Each entry is a URL currently being processed by a worker. Should be O(workers_per_shard) at steady state. A climb without a matching drop = leases not getting ack'd (worker crashes? frontier.ack failures?).
panels.title: inflight ZSET: items per shard

panels.description: Bytes per second of memory growth (positive) or shrinkage (negative). Use this to answer 'when did memory start growing' - overlay with a crawler-start annotation to attribute. Computed as rate(used_memory[5m]).
panels.title: Memory growth rate

panels.description: redis_memory_used_rss_bytes / redis_memory_used_bytes. 1.0 = perfect (kernel pages exactly match Redis's allocations). >1.5 = allocator holding pages Redis no longer wants; >2.0 = consider a Redis restart or tuning the allocator. Below 1.0 means swap (very bad).
panels.title: Memory fragmentation ratio

panels.description: Per-second rates of `evicted_keys_total` (eviction policy fired - Redis hit maxmemory and dropped keys) and `expired_keys_total` (TTL expired naturally). Cumulative versions exist as separate panels; the rates tell you if this is happening NOW vs in the past.
panels.title: Eviction + Expiration rates
